title: A service that runs
goal: One Spring Boot application, one pom.xml, one endpoint that returns JSON. Nothing distributed, no database, no Docker. You should be able to curl a response within the hour.
startWith: An empty folder and the tools from the Setup tab installed.

newIdeas.plain: A Maven dependency whose only job is to pull in a coherent set of libraries. spring-boot-starter-webmvc pulls in Tomcat, Jackson and Spring MVC together, at versions known to work with each other.

A pom.xml your pom.xml inherits from. spring-boot-starter-parent supplies the version number for every Spring library, so you never write versions yourself. That is the only pom you need until step 04.
A Java class declared in one line: record Wallet(UUID id, String label) {}. You get the constructor, getters, equals, hashCode and toString for free, and the fields cannot change after construction.

A folder convention: domain/ holds your business rules as plain Java, adapter/in/ holds the ways the outside world calls you (HTTP controllers), adapter/out/ holds the ways you call the outside world (database, other services). The rule is one-directional: domain imports nothing from the others.

tasks.why: You want the exact Maven and Java versions this project assumes, not whatever your IDE defaults to.
tasks.how: Run this from the folder that will hold the project. It downloads a zip and unpacks it into account-service/. If you would rather use the website, choose Maven, Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1.1, group io.ledgerflow, artifact account-service, and add the Spring Web and Spring Boot Actuator dependencies only.

blocks.label: Run this in Git Bash, in the folder above where the project should live
blocks.body:
curl -s https://start.spring.io/starter.zip \
  -d type=maven-project -d language=java -d javaVersion=25 \
  -d bootVersion=4.1.1 -d packaging=jar \
  -d groupId=io.ledgerflow -d artifactId=account-service \
  -d name=account-service -d packageName=io.ledgerflow.account \
  -d dependencies=web,actuator \
  -o account-service.zip

unzip -q account-service.zip -d account-service && rm account-service.zip
cd account-service

check.expect: You see mvnw, pom.xml and src/. Every command from here until step 04 runs from inside account-service/.

tasks.do: Read your pom.xml and confirm it is a single, parentless-but-for-Boot file
tasks.why: Half the confusion in Maven projects comes from not knowing which pom.xml is in charge. Right now there is exactly one, and it is this one.
tasks.how: Open pom.xml. The <parent> block points at spring-boot-starter-parent with <relativePath/> empty — that empty tag means "do not look on disk for the parent, fetch it from Maven Central". There is no aggregator pom, no <modules>, and no root pom above this folder. You do not need one until step 04, when there are two services to build together.

blocks.label: This is the whole build file — nothing else is required today
blocks.body:
<project>
  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.1</version>
    <relativePath/>            <!-- empty = resolve from Maven Central -->
  </parent>

  <groupId>io.ledgerflow</groupId>
  <artifactId>account-service</artifactId>
  <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>

  <properties><java.version>25</java.version></properties>

  <dependencies>
    <!-- Boot 4 renamed this: it is webmvc, not web -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build><plugins><plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  </plugin></plugins></build>
</project>

check.expect: Dependencies resolve and no version numbers of your own appear anywhere in the file.

tasks.why: Deciding where code goes now costs one command. Deciding it in step 12, across six services, costs a week.
tasks.how: The layout separates what the business does from how it talks to the world. domain/ is plain Java: no Spring imports, no JPA annotations, no Jackson. adapter/in/web is where HTTP arrives. adapter/out/persistence is where the database lives (empty until step 02). application/ holds use cases that orchestrate the domain. You will feel the benefit at step 02, when the database arrives and your business types do not have to change.

blocks.label: One command creates all of them

tasks.do: Write Account and Wallet as plain records in domain/model
tasks.why: These are the two things this service is about. They should be readable by someone who has never used Spring.
tasks.how: This is the answer to "what model am I building?" — it is a domain model: ordinary Java types describing the business, with no framework in them. Later steps add a second, different model for the database (step 02) and a third for events (step 08). Keeping them separate is deliberate; the notes in step 02 explain what it buys you.

blocks.label: src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/account/domain/model/Wallet.java
src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/account/domain/model/Account.java

check.expect: Prints 'clean'. If it prints an import, a framework has leaked into your domain.

tasks.do: Serve GET /api/v1/accounts from a hardcoded list
tasks.why: One endpoint proves the whole chain works — Maven, Boot, Tomcat, Jackson — before a database can confuse the diagnosis.
tasks.how: @RestController tells Spring this class handles HTTP and that return values become the response body. Jackson turns the records into JSON with no configuration. Note the fixed account id: every curl command in this project uses that UUID, so use exactly this one.

blocks.label: src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/account/adapter/in/web/AccountController.java

tasks.why: A service that has never served a request is not a service yet.
tasks.how: spring-boot:run starts the app in the foreground; leave it running and use a second terminal for curl. Stop it with Ctrl-C. If port 8080 is busy, something else is using it — the Setup tab shows how to find and stop it on Windows.

blocks.label: Terminal 1 — start the app, leave it running
If the endpoint 404s, check the app booted at all

proof.expect: A JSON array with one account and twenty wallets.
proof.note: If this works you have a running service. Resist adding anything else — no database, no second module, no Docker. The next step adds exactly one thing.

doneWhen: The endpoint returns JSON, and you have written zero infrastructure code.

lessons.title: Search Everywhere — double Shift
lessons.teach: Press Shift twice. One box finds classes, files, actions and settings. It is the only navigation shortcut you have to learn; the rest are shortcuts to parts of this one.

lessons.title: Navigate → Class (Ctrl+N)
lessons.teach: You are about to open Wallet.java. Don't hunt in the project tree — Ctrl+N, type Wallet, Enter. It matches camel humps, so WA finds WalletApplication.
lessons.fallbackTip: Ctrl+N (Navigate → Class), type the class name.

lessons.title: Run from the gutter
lessons.teach: Click the green ▶ next to main instead of the terminal. IntelliJ writes a run configuration for you; every later step reuses it.
